title: The 610 Office and the Golden Shield

text.brief: Three days after Jiang Zemin ordered a campaign against Falun Gong, the Party created an office on June 10, 1999 and named it for the date.
text.record: The ban followed on July 20, 1999. The 610 Office then ran arrests, forced conversion classes and camps for practitioners ([H. Res. 605, 111th Congress (govinfo)](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-111hres605ih/html/BILLS-111hres605ih.htm); [CECC hearing statement by Caylan Ford: Falun Gong in China, review and update (2012)](https://www.cecc.gov/sites/evo-subsites/cecc.house.gov/files/documents/hearings/2012/CECC%20Hearing%20Testimony%20-%20Caylan%20Ford%20-%2012.18.12.pdf)). The Ministry of Public Security built the Golden Shield Project in the same years to link surveillance and police databases across the country. Falun Gong practitioners sued Cisco in 2011 and alleged that the company built features into Golden Shield to identify and track them. The Ninth Circuit let most claims proceed on July 7, 2023, and Cisco asked the Supreme Court to review the ruling.
text.reading: The Party fused a political campaign with a police network and bought parts of the network abroad, which is Stratagem 3. An American appeals court held that a company can face trial for aiding abuse through the systems it sells, and the case turns on what Cisco knew and built.
text.gapText: Technology Architecture. Export rules covered crime-control items such as fingerprint gear but not the network equipment that runs a police state.
text.fix: Extend export controls to surveillance systems by function rather than by product list, and require sellers to screen for police end users.
